data.title: Perioral dermatitis — viva
data.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Perioral dermatitis** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. What is perioral dermatitis?**
- Common facial eruption of young women (and children) with small erythematous papules, papulovesicles and pustules on a red, scaly background around the mouth, sparing a narrow zone at the vermilion border; may involve nasolabial folds and periocular areas (periorificial dermatitis)

**Q2. Causes/triggers.**
- Topical (and inhaled/nasal) corticosteroids — the most important; heavy moisturisers/foundation, fluorinated toothpaste, cosmetics, sunscreens; OCPs, hormonal changes; Demodex, Candida, fusobacteria (unclear); barrier dysfunction/atopy
- Granulomatous periorificial dermatitis (childhood — Afro-Caribbean children, yellow-brown papules; FACE — facial Afro-Caribbean childhood eruption)

**Q3. Differential diagnosis.**
- Rosacea (older, central face, flushing, telangiectasia), acne (comedones), seborrhoeic dermatitis (greasy scale, nasolabial), contact dermatitis (allergic — patch test), steroid rosacea, Demodex folliculitis, lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei, sarcoidosis (granulomatous form), impetigo, lip-licking dermatitis

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Spongiotic dermatitis with perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, sometimes rosacea-like; granulomatous variant shows non-caseating granulomas around follicles

**Q5. Treatment.**
- 'Zero therapy': stop all topical steroids and facial cosmetics (warn about rebound flare for 1–2 weeks; taper from potent to hydrocortisone if severe), use gentle cleanser
- Topical: metronidazole 0.75–1% gel/cream, erythromycin, clindamycin, azelaic acid 15–20%, pimecrolimus/tacrolimus (also for steroid withdrawal), ivermectin 1%
- Oral: doxycycline 40–100 mg or minocycline for 6–12 weeks (adults); erythromycin/azithromycin in children and pregnancy; isotretinoin (resistant)
- Recurrence is common if steroids are restarted

**Q6. Describe the clinical features in detail.**
- Young women (also children): grouped small (1–2 mm) erythematous papules, papulovesicles and pustules on a red, mildly scaly base around the mouth, nasolabial folds and chin, characteristically sparing a narrow zone of skin next to the vermilion border; periocular/perinasal variants ('periorificial dermatitis'); burning more than itching

**Q7. What is granulomatous periorificial dermatitis?**
- Childhood variant (prepubertal, often darker skin) with yellow-brown monomorphic papules around mouth, nose, eyes; histology granulomatous; treat with topical metronidazole/erythromycin, oral erythromycin (children <8 y) or azithromycin

**Q8. Why do topical steroids worsen it?**
- Steroids give initial improvement (vasoconstriction, anti-inflammation) but cause rebound flare on stopping and perpetuate barrier damage, follicular overgrowth of Demodex/fusiform bacteria — steroid addiction; must stop all facial steroids (taper potent ones or switch to hydrocortisone/tacrolimus) — 'zero therapy'

**Q9. What doses of oral tetracyclines are used?**
- Doxycycline 50–100 mg/day or minocycline 50–100 mg/day for 6–12 weeks, tapering; erythromycin/azithromycin in children and pregnancy

## Quick spotter facts
- Papulopustules around the mouth sparing the vermilion border in a steroid-cream user — perioral dermatitis
- Zero therapy + doxycycline

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Rosacea and related disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
